chapters.summary: Chair Carmen De La Rosa welcomes attendees to the oversight hearing on NYC 311, describes it as a 24/7 non-emergency connection to city government, and notes its 2003 launch as a centralized call center.
chapters.title: De La Rosa opens 311 oversight hearing and introduces system

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to our oversight hearing on 311.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Carmen De La Rosa, Chair of the Committee on Technology, and today we will be discussing New York City's 311 system.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: NYC 311 is New York City's 24-hour, 7-day-a-week, non-emergency services connecting New Yorkers and visitors with city government.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Providing necessary information and taking complaints.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa explains that 311 now handles millions of interactions via phone, text, app, and website in more than 175 languages, making it the largest 311 system in the country.
chapters.title: De La Rosa describes 311's evolution into multi-channel platform

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Launched in 2003 as a centralized telephone call center, 301 has evolved significantly over the past two decades, expanding the ways in which the public can communicate with city government as technology and public expectations have changed.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Today, 311 handles millions of interactions each year through phone calls, text messages, its mobile application, and website, providing assistance in more than 175 languages as the largest 311 system in the country.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: NYC 311 plays an essential role in making city government more accessible and responsive to the people it serves.

chapters.summary: Chair says New Yorkers rely on 311 for issues from parking to heat complaints, that it routes complaints to agencies, and that its data supports open data analysis and resource allocation.
chapters.title: De La Rosa outlines 311's role in service requests and open data

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: New Yorkers rely on 311 for a broad range of issues, from questions about parking regulation and sanitation services to filing complaints about heat or hot water in their building.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In many instances, 311 serves as a starting point for resolving an issue by directing a complaint to the appropriate city agency for action.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Today, 311 is more than a customer service system.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The information generated through millions of service requests provide an important source of data for city agencies, elected officials, researchers, advocates, and members of the public through the city's open data portal.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The data can help identify patterns in service, delivery, inform discussions about allocations of resources, highlight community needs, and reveal areas where the city may...

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: May be improved.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa argues 311 must be continually improved and modernized as a tool for accountability and communication between New Yorkers and local government.
chapters.title: De La Rosa calls for modernizing 311 and accountability

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Given the central role of 311 plays in the day-to-day functioning of our city, we must continually examine how the system can be improved and modernized.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: 311 should serve as a tool for accountability and communication between New Yorkers and local government.

chapters.summary: Chair lists Intro 173 by Councilmember Dinowitz on GPS coordinates, Intro 669 by Deputy Speaker Williams on traffic complaints to NYPD Transportation Bureau, and Intro 800 by Councilmember Schulman on redirecting requests.
chapters.title: De La Rosa outlines three 311 bills under consideration

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Today we will be considering three bills intended to improve New York City 311 and the services it provides.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Intro 173 by Councilmember Dinowitz in relation to the use of global positioning systems, coordinates for 311 complaints and service requests.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Intro 669 by Deputy Speaker Williams in relation to referring 311.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: 111 non-emergency traffic condition complaints to the Transportation Bureau of the Police Department,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: and Intro 800 by Councilmember Shulman, requiring the 311 Customer Service Center to redirect requests for services or complaints to the appropriate agencies.

chapters.summary: Chair thanks committee staff and recognizes Councilmembers Gutierrez, Dinowitz, and Schulman, noting more than 15 other 311 bills are not being heard today but remain important to the Council.
chapters.title: De La Rosa thanks staff, recognizes members, notes other 311 bills

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing from the administration, advocates, and members of the public about these bills, as well as broader opportunities to make NYC 311 more resilient, accessible, user-friendly, and effective for all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'd like to thank the committee's staff, policy analyst Eric Brown, legislative counsel Irina Babosky, and chief of staff James Burke and Hiba Imad for working in and putting this hearing together.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'd like to recognize technology committee members, Councilmember Juan Gutierrez, and we've also been joined by Councilmember Dinowitz and Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I will say there are more than 15 other bills that we're not considering today on 311.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So even though we're light on folks today, I want to be sure to emphasize that 311 is an important issue that this council cares about.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Specifically, there's a lot of legislation to try and make it work a little better.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Eric Dinowitz thanks the chair and recounts COVID-era wellness calls where seniors raised quality-of-life issues like noise and sidewalk cracks, showing these concerns persist even during crises.
chapters.title: Dinowitz begins remarks on quality of life and 311

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'll now turn to Councilmember Dinowitz to deliver his opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Lynn also reached.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We weren't sure who you were going to call first.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for the hearing and for hearing my bill.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Of all the issues we face in our city, the one that rises to the top time and again is quality of life.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'm often reminded of this because...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: During COVID, during the height of when there was fear surrounding all of us.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I was doing, before I was in office, doing wellness calls to our older adults.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I started out these calls expecting to hear the tragic stories of people losing loved ones, being afraid to go out to get eggs and milk.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the vast majority of my calls really were about quality of life, were about the noise or about the cracks in the sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They wanted to go out for a walk and the cracks in the sidewalks were preventing them from safely doing that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, illegal dumping places.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So, you know, I think about this because at the height.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Of when fear and death was permeating our city, quality of life still rose to the top as this critical issue for many New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz lists potholes, running hydrants, broken street lamps, flooded homes, and broken park fences as unresolved issues, arguing 311 needs improvement to address safety and dignity.
chapters.title: Dinowitz describes quality-of-life failures and need for 311 improvement

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And quality of life speaks to our ability to live with safety and with dignity in our own city.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Streets.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Rife with potholes, hydrants that are running and wasting water, darkened streets due to broken street lamps, flooded homes due to blocked sewer lines, broken fences in our parks.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: These are just...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Some of the quality of life issues that were not addressed do impact that safety and quality of life and dignity that we cherish so much.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Here in New York City, of course, we have 311, a system through which New Yorkers can report and address our quality of life concerns.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But we know 311 is in need of improvement.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz introduces Intro 173 to require GPS pin-drop location for 311 complaints, citing a missing hydrant repaired down the block, an unaddressed service road, and overpass lights unfixed because location could not be found.
chapters.title: Dinowitz presents Intro 173 and examples of 311 location failures

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Today we are discussing my bill, Intro 173, which will require 311 to use GPS data to pinpoint exactly where a constituent wants to report their issue.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Time and again, constituents call my office because 311 was used, but the city agency either couldn't find a location or went to the wrong location.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We had a missing hydrant reported, but DEP repaired a separate hydrant down the block.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: On a service road in my district, a constituent was unable to file a 3-in-1 complaint because the stretches on the service road have no street address.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Lights on an overpass in my district were out.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Because there was no address on the overpass, the constituent called 311 instead of using the app.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The report was logged manually, and three months later, the lights were still out.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And when there was follow-up done, we eventually were given the response that the lights weren't fixed because the location could not be found.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A constituent who reported a blocked sewer line had to describe it as 100 feet from his house toward the direction of the sewer plant, which is hardly an efficient way to describe a location.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Bell Tower Park in Riverdale had a broken sidewalk and the constituent had to use the nearest address, which isn't really close to this bell tower.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz shares more examples of constituents struggling to describe locations, including a blocked sewer and Bell Tower Park sidewalk, and says precise GPS capability would make 311 more efficient and responsive.
chapters.title: Dinowitz argues GPS location will make 311 more responsive

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There are obviously more cases in my office alone.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Each of us in the council has dealt with similar issues.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Countless New Yorkers who haven't called our offices have dealt with this issue time and again.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: As New Yorkers, we deserve a more responsive and efficient experience with our government.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If 311 is the vehicle by which New Yorkers address their quality of life concerns, we must ensure that it is as efficient and responsive to the needs of our constituents as possible.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Adding precise GPS location ability would allow for that to happen.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Intro 173 would allow for that to happen.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Lynn Schulman speaks in support of Intro 800, which would create a dedicated 311 category for complaints about city jail conditions and require public tracking and status updates for accountability.
chapters.title: Schulman introduces Intro 800 on tracking jail-condition complaints

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And now I turn over to Council Member Shulman for her opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Today I'm here to speak in support of my bill, Intro 800.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This legislation would create a clearer, more transparent way to track complaints about conditions in our city jails.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Currently, when someone in a city jail has a complaint about the conditions of their confinement, there is not a clear public-facing system for tracking that complaint from submission through resolution.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Without that transparency, it can be difficult to know whether a complaint was received, whether it was referred to the appropriate personnel, or whether the underlying issue was ultimately addressed.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: My legislation would require the Department of Information, Technology, and Telecommunications to establish a dedicated 311 service request category for complaints and service requests related to conditions in city jails.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It would also require the city to publish records of those requests and provide updates on their status.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This legislation is fundamentally about accountability.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: A transparent system for receiving and tracking complaints can help identify recurring problems, ensure that concerns are directed to the appropriate personnel, and provide the public with greater visibility into how these issues are being addressed.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Everyone in our city deserves to be treated with dignity, including people who are incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I believe this legislation is an important step toward greater transparency and accountability and toward ensuring that our city jails are humane and habitable.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair De La Rosa reads a statement from Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams supporting Intro 669, which would route non-emergency traffic complaints like drag racing, speeding, and truck violations to the NYPD Transportation Bureau.
chapters.title: De La Rosa reads Deputy Speaker Williams' statement on Intro 669

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I will now read a statement on behalf of Deputy Speaker Dr.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Nantasha Williams.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: members of the Committee on Technology for the opportunity to submit testimony on Intro 669.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: New Yorkers rely on 311 as their primary point of contact with city government.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: When residents take the time to report a concern, they should have the confidence that the complaint will reach the agency position to respond.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In Southeast Queens, traffic concerns are among the issues residents raise with my office regularly.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We hear about chronic speeding on residential streets, illegal truck traffic, dangerous driving, congestion, and other conditions that affect both quality of life and public safety.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Many of these are not isolated incidents.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: They are recurring problems that residents experience day after day.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Intro 669 would require NYC 311 to refer non-emergency traffic condition complaints to NYPD Transportation Bureau.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: This includes complaints involving drag racing, chronic speeding, congestion, gridlock, truck route violations, and other non-emergency traffic conditions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The goal is simple.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: When New Yorkers report a traffic concern, that complaint should have a clear path to an agency responsible for addressing it.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Residents should not have to repeatedly report the same condition without understanding where the complaint is going or whether an appropriate agency has received it.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: 311 should be more than a system that generates service request numbers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It should help residents navigate city government, help agencies identify recurring conditions, and create a clearer connection between a complaint and a city response.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Better routing is an important part of making the system more useful.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: and accountable.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing from the administration about how traffic-related complaints are currently handled through 311, where gaps may exist, and how the city can improve coordination when residents report recurring traffic conditions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I thank the chair and the committee for hearing Intro 669 and for examining how we make 311 more responsive and effective for all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In service, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Natasha Williams.

chapters.summary: Chair announces OTI testimony will be followed by public testimony, welcomes Joe Morrisroe, OTI Deputy Commissioner for 311, and staff administers the affirmation to tell the truth.
chapters.title: De La Rosa welcomes OTI Deputy Commissioner Joe Morrisroe and administers oath

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We thank our Deputy Speaker for her statement, and today we will hear testimony from the Office of Technology and Innovation, followed by testimonies from the public.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I now want to welcome Joe Morris-Roe, OTI Deputy Commissioner for 311.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Before we begin, I just kindly want to request you to raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth and respond honestly to Council Member's questions?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You can start your testimony.

chapters.summary: Joe Morrisroe introduces himself as Deputy Commissioner of NYC 311, notes 20 years overseeing its transformation from call center to multi-channel platform, and says he will discuss operations, successes, and proposed legislation.
chapters.title: Morrisroe introduces himself and 311's transformation

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair De La Rosa and members of the City Council Committee on Technology.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: My name is Joe Morrisrow, and I am the Deputy Commissioner of New York City 311.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Over the last 20 years, I have overseen New York City 311's transformation from a call center to the multi-channel, multilingual platform that it is today.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'm pleased to join the committee today to discuss our operations, highlight our

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: recent successes and discuss today's proposed legislation.

chapters.summary: Morrisroe says 311 is available 24/7 via call center, online portal, text, app, and social media; received 37 million contacts in 2025; and earned 93% customer satisfaction with 90% likely to recommend.
chapters.title: Morrisroe reports 311 volume and customer satisfaction statistics

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: As you know, NYC 311 delivers fast and easy access to government services and information with the highest possible level of customer service.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: 311 is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year, through multiple channels, including the call center,

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: online portal, text, mobile application, and social media.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Originally launched as a call center, New York City 311 has evolved into the most comprehensive municipal government customer service platform in the nation.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: 311 received 37 million customer contacts in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And on an annual basis receives more calls than all U.S.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: City 311 call centers combined.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'm also pleased to share with the Council a recent report by an independent third party on the public satisfaction with New York City 311.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Call center representatives received a customer satisfaction rating of 93%.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And 90% of the respondents stated they are likely to recommend 311, which outperforms best-in-class private sector companies.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The level of public satisfaction is a testament to the dedication and the commitment of the New York City 311 team that serves their fellow New Yorkers every day.

chapters.summary: Morrisroe describes 311 outcomes: providing information, referring externally, or submitting service requests to designated agencies. He says 311 cannot create requests unilaterally and relies on agency partnerships, feedback, and the RSAT dashboard.
chapters.title: Morrisroe explains service request routing and agency collaboration

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It is important to note that 311 serves as the platform to provide information and services to the public.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: With few exceptions, public interactions with 311

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: and result in one of the following outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The customer has an information request, such as a garbage pickup day, and the information is provided.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: A customer is referred to an external entity, which can include a utility or a state or federal agency.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And a customer's inquiry is submitted as a service request,

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: to the designated agency and a confirmation tracking number is provided.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We rely on our collaborative relationships with each city agency to build out service request forms and information pages, which we also call knowledge articles, those that properly reflect the mission and services for each agency or office.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: 311 does not create service requests unilaterally.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: There must be an agency that will accept the request, investigate, and if applicable, undertake appropriate action or resolution.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Once a service request is submitted through New York City 311, it becomes the responding agency's responsibility to address and respond.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: When an agency decides that amending a current service request or adding a new one is necessary, it contacts 311 to create, test, and deploy a service request form.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Agency feedback partially informs the update we implement to the entire 311 platform.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: User feedback is also extremely useful to us, which is why we deploy customer surveys that inform the Resolution Satisfaction Dashboard, which goes by the acronym RSAT, which is available on the site.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We also value the input we receive from council members as frequent 311 users, and I'm happy to continue the conversation.

chapters.summary: Morrisroe says 311 currently collects GPS coordinates when location services are enabled and otherwise uses entered addresses. He supports exploring a pin-drop geolocator with ESRI to identify addresses in agency-required formats.
chapters.title: Morrisroe addresses Intro 173 GPS pin-drop proposal

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I will now turn to the legislation associated with this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Intro 173 would require the use of Global Positioning System, GPS, coordinates for 311 service requests.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We agree that our user interface would be improved with the capability to capture a user's coordinates with the familiar pin drop that many location-based applications use.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Currently, 311 service request collect GPS coordinates, latitude and longitude, based on the customer enabling location services in the mobile app or on the website,

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: and the customer confirming the address that is identified.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: If location services functionality is disabled, 311 collects latitude and longitude based on the address entered by the customer.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We have been exploring how our geolocator service could collect lat and long based on a pin drop

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Then identify the address in the format required by the agency based on the service request.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: For example, an address, an intersection, or a block face.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I am looking forward to working with the council to find the best path forward for this enhancement.

chapters.summary: Morrisroe explains that emergency traffic calls transfer to 911 and non-emergency calls generate service requests routed to NYPD precincts. He says OTI cannot comment on the policy merits and urges Council to discuss with NYPD.
chapters.title: Morrisroe addresses Intro 669 traffic complaint routing

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Introduction 669 proposes to refer 311 non-emergency traffic condition complaints to the Transportation Bureau of the Police Department.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: As I noted above, we work with each agency to develop service requests to work best for the customer and agency policies and workflows that support their responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: For the types of complaints listed in this legislation, the protocol is similar.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: If a customer describes an emergency condition in progress, the call is transferred to 911.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: A call describing a non-emergency situation will generate a service request that is routed to the appropriate NYPD precinct.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: NYPD has determined that this is the course of action to occur for such complaints.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: While the New York City 301 system is capable of changing the way such complaints are routed,

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Neither OTI nor 311 can comment on the merits of the proposal, as the underlying policy and procedures belong to NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: My colleagues at the NYPD have told us that they believe many of the calls contemplated by the bill should be routed through 911 and that many would call for responses from other bureaus within the department.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Therefore, I urge the Council to discuss this proposal directly with NYPD, who would be happy to meet with the sponsors.

chapters.summary: Morrisroe says most service requests are correctly assigned but exceptions exist, such as street cave-ins initially sent to DOT before reassignment. He says information on responsible agency is available within 10 days and 311 is exploring solutions.
chapters.title: Morrisroe addresses Intro 800 redirects and cave-in example

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And finally, Intro 800 would require New York City 311 to redirect service requests to the appropriate agency.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: While a vast majority of service requests are appropriately assigned and routed to agencies, there are some exceptions that it appears this legislation is seeking to address.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: A common example is when a customer reports a street cave-in.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: of Transportation, or DOT, initially investigates reports of cave-ins, determines who is responsible for restoring the roadway, and then refers the cave-in to that agency or utility for repair.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Information about the agency or utility responsible for repairing the cave-in will be available within 10 days of submitting a service request.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That said, I do understand the customer's frustration when this occurs, which is why we have been identifying solutions for these kinds of scenarios.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'm happy to talk you through how we have been thinking about implementing solutions to this problem and align on the best next steps to make this process better for New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Morrisroe thanks the committee on behalf of the 311 team and says he will now take council members' questions.
chapters.title: Morrisroe concludes testimony and offers to take questions

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: In closing, on behalf of the dedicated team at 311, thank you again for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I will now take council members'questions.

chapters.summary: Chair De La Rosa thanks Morrisroe for 20 years of service, notes the Council has many 311 bills, and contrasts the 93% satisfaction rating with constituents reporting unresolved service requests. She announces questions on staffing.
chapters.title: De La Rosa opens Q&A on 311 staffing and service complaints

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I just want to say 20 years is a long time, so we thank you for your service.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And we're looking forward to this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: As I mentioned, there's a ton of bills that the council wants to pursue around 311.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And I think Dino had said it best, my neighbor to the north, that, you know, our constituents are often calling us about quality of life issues.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And, you know, 93%, I think you said, satisfaction rating is impressive.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It doesn't feel like that on the street.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I feel like we get the brunt of folks telling us, like, service requests are being closed and not being fixed.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And I know that there is a process.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So we hope today to dig into some of those questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And I know we've been joined by my colleague from the Bronx, Councilmember Riley, as well.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a few questions about staffing, and then I'm going to open it for committee members for questions, and then I'll come back.

chapters.summary: Chair asks about current headcount. Morrisroe says there are 248 budgeted call center representatives, no dedicated CCRs for the website, and app support is shared across OTI teams; he will follow up with estimates.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about 311 headcount for call center, website, and app

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But what is the present headcount for 311?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The budgeted headcount is 248 call center representatives.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We use the term CCR, and that's the folks who are on the front line answering calls.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So those are the call center operators, 248.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And how many work on the 311 website?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We don't have any call center representatives on the 311 website.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's actually supported by folks at 311 as well as the broader OTI team.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, and about how many?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I would have to come back and come up with a figure because it's a work that's done by different people and it's piece part work.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So I don't have a single answer for that, but it's something we could estimate for you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If you could come back to us, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And what about on the 311 mobile app?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That would be similar to the website where there's a group of folks both on the, we call it the business side, right, the three-on-one side as well as the application side.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We had a number of 10 people, but we're not sure if that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We can check that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Morrisroe says texts are handled manually by call center representatives, automation has been explored but current Q&A works well, there are 53 CCR vacancies, and starting salary is $40,600.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about text messaging, automation, vacancies, and salary

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Text messages, same answer, sort of.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate that question because I can give a little bit more context on that one.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The text message is...

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: are handled by the same call center representatives that handle calls.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's part of the broader call center representative group.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And then is that process, the text messaging process, automated or are people manually replying to text messages?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: They are manually replying.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: When someone texts 311, which you can do by texting 311-692, 311-NYC, that request is going to be served by a person, by someone who works at 311, a call center representative.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Is there a plan to automate the process?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We have looked at different plans that would automate that, ideally for something that would serve the customer better.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: For now, though, the Q&A, as we call it, serves very well for customers.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We get very good quality scores, customer satisfaction scores in that area.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And there is that element of kind of back and forth questions.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So the customer knows that they're dealing with a representative as opposed to perhaps an automated assistant.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And how many vacancies are there at 311 right now?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Currently, as of this week, there are 53 vacancies in the call center representative position.

chapters.summary: Morrisroe says call takers are not outsourced but 311 uses overflow vendor King Teleservices daily as backup. The contract was extended through February 28, 2027, and he will provide the exact contract value later.
chapters.title: De La Rosa questions outsourcing and King Teleservices contract

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you know what's the starting salary for a co-sensor representative?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's $40,600 a year.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: More than paraprofessionals.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Did the number of call takers change in the last two years?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Over the last two years, the budgeted headcount has been 248.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's been consistent.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, it's consistent.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And what about outsourcing?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Are call takers outsourced?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The 311 call takers or call center representatives themselves are not outsourced.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: However, the agency has a contract with an overflow vendor that's based in Brooklyn to handle calls.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Which is the vendor?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The vendor is King Teleservices, Inc., K-I-N-G.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Tell us.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: King Teleservices.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And then you said, so that's for an overflow if the number is higher than capacity.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we use that vendor as what we call our overflow vendor.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: They are trained to do the same work that the city 311 call center staff does.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And when is that overflow triggered?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So they actually operate in a steady state.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So they take calls every day.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So in that way, we have a baseline that there's always going to be someone there.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The vendor serves as one of our backup locations, basically our content.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: of operations plan.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So if something were to happen, we have the ability to have that vendor kind of hot and ready as opposed to having to stand them up so that they are in effect every day.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Are those the folks who work for the vendor paid the same as the city workers?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I don't have the answer on how much they are paid.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The city has a contract with the vendor.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We pay what we call a production hour rate.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's the information that we would have.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The vendor as a private company would work that arrangement with their employees.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Was the contract, the contract term, we have information that the contract term was ending February 2026.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We're now in September 2026.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Was the contract renewed with King Teleservice?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That is a very timely question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The current contract that we're in was extended last year for the period March of 2026 through February 28th of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: There is no extension on that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The expiration date is March 2027.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The current end date of the contract we're under ends in March 2020.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'm sorry, February 28, 2027.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, and what is the contract value?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you know?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The contract value, it's...

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I would have to get back to you to the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The contract has had different iterations over the years, so I would want to zero in on what the current one is.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'm going to stop there for now.

chapters.summary: Schulman notes confusion about Intro 800's committee, then asks about new 311 regulations around homelessness. Morrisroe says encampment requests now route exclusively to DSS, while other homeless outreach calls have long gone to DSS.
chapters.title: Schulman questions 311 homelessness regulations and encampment routing

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I have a lot more questions, but I want to open to Councilmember Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So the statement I read was for a different 311 bill.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: There was some confusion as to what was on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, anyway.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I caught it, but then I was like.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I just caught it now.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I have a different bill that's going to be in another committee.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: For people who are incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This one I don't have questions on.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I do have an oversight question, though, Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So the new regulations around 311 and homelessness, can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Because I will tell you that in my district there's confusion in the NYPD as to what exactly it is and isn't.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate the question, and I appreciate the clarification on Intro 800.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yeah, Intro 800 is fine.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Well, we could– it's fine.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: With respect to the question on the homeless handling and–

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I can speak to the 311 piece where we play a role, which is to perform the intake from our customer's request, which could be the calls they could call.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: They could do some mobile app or they could go online.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then our job is to get that request to the responding agency.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: In this case, as of recent, the responding agency for an encampment request, which I believe you're referring to, does route now to the Department of Social Services, DSS.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Exclusively, right?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Not...

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Clarify.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Exclusively to DSS.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And other 311 calls in terms of people that are homeless on the street other than an encampment, that still goes to NYPD?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: For other calls, we typically refer to what's known as homeless outreach assistance or homeless service assistance.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So if it's more of an individual in need of support services.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Those currently go and have gone directly to, I say DHS, I should say DSS, Department of Social Services.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So there's been no change in that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Those continue to go to DSS.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.title: Schulman asks for definition of encampment and requests information

utterances.text: Yeah, my questions are more like for NYPD now because your role is your role, so that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Let me ask just one question about...

utterances.text: That would be very helpful because we get asked questions about that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member Dinnowitz.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz recalls Morrisroe's April 2024 testimony about an ESRI geolocator and asks whether it is now in use. Morrisroe confirms the current state and says work continues with ESRI to collect pin-drop coordinates and pass them to agencies.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks about ESRI geolocator and GPS pin-drop progress

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you for coming for your testimony, Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to ask first about the GPS location.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: On April 25th, 2024, if you can remember back that far, you had testified that NYC 311 is exploring a new geolocator, ESRI.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Which is you referenced in your testimony today, the service that will take a step further and collect latitude and longitude based on a pin drop, then identify the address in the format required by the agency based on the service report.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I just want to make sure that's the format that's being used now.

chapters.summary: Morrisroe says 311 is working with ESRI on a public-facing pin-drop tool that can also deliver coordinates in agency-required formats. Dinowitz says if it is good enough for Uber, it is good enough for New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Morrisroe explains support for GPS pin-drop like Uber or Lyft

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for the question and the background.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate the timing, the date reminder.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Yes, that's the current state that we're in now.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So this is different.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I want to just explain the difference between what you're describing, your testimony about using geolocation to find an address, and the actual problem

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: that so many of our constituents are facing, that is that latitude longitude doesn't always line up with an address.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So what steps is the 301 prepared to make to actually...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: really use the geolocation, not to align it to necessarily an address, but to GPS coordinates, much as you would

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, if you're getting an Uber or Lyft.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And again, for the context around that, it's helpful.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's the work that we're doing, the work that I referenced in the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's the work that we're continuing with our partner, ESRI, use that acronym, to determine how we can do that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: For the public side, for the customer side, but then also be able to collect that and pass that to the agencies in the format that they need.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's the crux of the work that's underway.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, but just to be clear, essentially you are supportive of the bill.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We are supportive of the GPS locator, the pin drop locator.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Pin drop locator.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If it's good enough for Uber, it's good enough for a New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Right.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz notes his law required customer satisfaction surveys and says internal surveys show only about 33-35% satisfaction, while Morrisroe cited 93% from a third party. Morrisroe explains the third-party CFI Group survey measures experience with the call center representative, not whether the underlying problem was fixed.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions discrepancy between 93% and 33% satisfaction scores

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I have one other question.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I may come back to the GPS, but in your testimony, you said you're pleased to share with the council a report by an independent third party on the public satisfaction with NYC 311, that it's a rating of

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: customer satisfaction rating of 93%.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A little while back, I passed legislation that required customer satisfaction feedback surveys to be done at the end of the calls or allow people on the app to fill those out.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And on that, in your internal surveys, the customer satisfaction, just looking at it now, is 33% strongly or agree or regularly agree.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That they're satisfied.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can you explain the discrepancy between the system that we enacted per law and this outside firm that you hired for customer satisfaction?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we'll start.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: There's two sides, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So I'll start on the information that I shared.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The customer satisfaction survey that we do is a third party resource.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: CFI Group Inc.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's their name.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: They are the leaders in American Customer Satisfaction Index survey in science.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We've been using them for several years.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's a really nice independent approach to having someone.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Contact customers who have interacted with the 311 call center.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's a pretty robust survey, multiple questions, and pretty robust response, statistically valid response rate.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And that's...

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Their methodology is what evaluates how the customer feels about their experience with the 311 call center representative.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, so I just want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The representative themselves, we're talking about satisfaction with their interaction with the representative, not necessarily their satisfaction with the way their service request was fixed or not fixed.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That is fair.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'll amend it just slightly, the experience with the representative themselves, but also that whole 311 experience, right?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Calling, reaching, having the conversation, that the rep is polite and professional, all of that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's what that score is for.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I think that's an important clarification.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You hire great people who have very good interactions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And at the same time, people's quality of life concerns, only 35% satisfaction score are really addressed in the meaningful way.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And that was the purpose behind that previous legislation, to make sure there's transparency around how the service requests are being not handled by the call service person, but handled really by the agency if the problem itself was fixed.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Both things could be true at the same time, that the person on the other end of the line is great and the agency didn't live up to the standards we expect.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So that was a previous 311 bill that I passed that I think really sheds a lot of light on this.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And this other one going forward, the GPS location, is going to make life a lot easier for New Yorkers, maybe even get that satisfaction score on your website up.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Chair De La Rosa thanks Dinowitz and calls on Councilmember Riley. Riley says a request marked closed does not mean the problem is fixed and asks whether the city measures resolution. Morrisroe explains the RSAT resolution satisfaction survey sent after a service request is closed.
chapters.title: Riley questions closed 311 requests and resolution metrics

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Good points.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I pass it on to Councilmember Gutierrez, followed by Riley.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Oh, and we've been joined by Councilmember Honey as well.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Riley.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair, and thank you so much, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I have another hearing I have to run to.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner, it was great seeing you and hearing your presentation.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Just to follow up on my colleague from the Bronx, Councilmember Dinowitz, a request marked closed does not necessarily mean that the underlying problem has been fixed,

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: and that's a concern that we're hearing from many constituents that come to our office, that they'll put in a 311 complaint and then miraculously it's closed, but the issue isn't fixed.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So does the city have any performance measures that they assess whether 311 requests are being resolved?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate the question, and I can actually leverage Councilmember Dinowitz's previous update to provide some context around that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So as I mentioned, we do have the front-end survey, which I described, but the survey that Councilmember Dinowitz mentioned, we kind of have a shorthand for it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We call it Resolution Satisfaction Survey.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It has an acronym, RSAT.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That gets at what you just asked.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: When a customer submits a service request to 311 and provides contact information, typically an email address, after that service request is closed by the responding agency, a survey is generated to that customer.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It can be a one-question answer or a three-question answer.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Basically, it comes down to were you satisfied?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's just the one question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: If the answer was no, it gives them an option to explain why.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That information is then collected, and that's what's posted on the city website under what we call the RSAT dashboard.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And that's what Councilmember Dinenwitz was referencing.

chapters.summary: Riley asks whether the city uses 311 data to identify repeated issues like illegal dumping or broken streetlights. Morrisroe says complaints are captured in NYC Open Data and shared with agencies, though he cannot speak to each agency's internal analysis tools.
chapters.title: Riley asks whether 311 identifies repeated complaint patterns

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Repeated complaints about the same location of issues can be a signal or persistent service failure that individual case closures may not address.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And aggravated 301 data could help agencies identify patterns and take preventative broader action.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So does the city identify patterns across individual 301 complaints?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: For example, repeated reports of illegal dumping, broken street lights, dangerous traffic conditions.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is there any way that you could use that information to prop agencies'actions and their responses?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate the question, and I can talk to that a bit.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'll do the 311 side first.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So all complaints are captured, and then the vast majority of those complaints are available on what's known as NYC Open Data, which then allows you to do location information, you know, a borough, a zip code, but right down to an address

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: so that the city as well as the public can track that to understand what's repeatedly there or if there is a common trend or anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That information also goes to each agency that accepts the service request.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So while I can't speak to the agency's tools and practice in terms of how they identify not only their work,

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: but in this case, they repeat or recurring locations, the information that 311 provides is there.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: 301 is an amazing asset to everyday New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think, you know, we always refer our constituents to utilize it.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So just making sure that it works a little bit more efficiently is something that we're always trying to gear towards.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm looking forward to continue working with you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Jennifer Gutierrez asks whether OTI or 311 has been informed about the Office of Community Safety folding in the Office to End Gender-Based Violence and whether call center reps might face delays redirecting calls.
chapters.title: Gutierrez questions Office of Community Safety consolidation and call routing

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Gutierrez.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Good to see you, Joe.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: One ties into a topic the council heard earlier today in the women and gender equity hearing.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Just curious from your side, the...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Office of Community Safety is now the umbrella office that is kind of folding in a bunch of other offices, one of which is the mayor's office to end gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I had asked today earlier in the hearing if, because of this new classification, essentially they're still working out through kind of

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: what the new office will look like for them, if they have communicated to OTI or 311 about kind of what a call would look like now serving under not its own separate office, but under...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You know, a whole nother office and whether or not that would place a delay on a call center representative potentially if they're in the know or not.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So I just wanted to ask you, how up to date are you kind of on this office consolidation?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And do you know if there's any reason?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And for, you know, a two, three second delay in a call center representative potentially kind of redirecting a call now that it's not a standalone office.

chapters.summary: Morrisroe says the Office of Community Safety has visited 311 and discussions are underway. He describes the Agency Relations team, which maintains contacts with every city agency and updates 311 content when policies or programs change.
chapters.title: Morrisroe explains Agency Relations and 311 content updates

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for the question and especially for the timely this morning update.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: They scheduled it perfectly.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So I can speak to the first part of your question, which is essentially, have we been in touch?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I think if I can frame it that way.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We've actually had the office 2311, as you know, as you know from the location.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we've not only had them on site to see our operation, but have started discussions about the work that they're doing, how 311 can help and inform that work, and how we would be a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You've had the Office of Community Safety come see you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Office of Community Safety, correct.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Well, there's, I mean, I think there's still.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: To my understanding, I feel like they're kind of restructuring and I don't know, I don't I don't think what we we know today, September 30th, I'm not sure if it will look structured the same way.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So that's and I know that oftentimes, even when the council passes new legislation, right, if that communication is not directed to 311, but not necessarily changing the way that these service requests are captured.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: They've visited.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You've been in communication.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you feel like, I don't know, was it a constructive conversation?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there any reason for New Yorkers to feel like, I don't know if I can call 311 now for this because now they're a subset.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: They're not even a standalone office anymore.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate that distinction there.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So I will say yes.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: My colleague came, my peer colleague came for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We've had those discussions.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But more importantly and more structurally, the 311 process works well in this situation.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we have a group called Agency Relations.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: They deal with every city agency, a number of state and federal agencies, but every city agency, every office, every mayor's office, there's a contact.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And the purpose of that is to exchange information such as a new program, a new policy, and make sure it gets into the 311 system.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So if there's something that's not there, we have vehicles that identify that, and then we raise it up with the agency.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And if the agency has something new, or even if they're not sure what they do or may not have, they come to 311, and then that's when our collaborative work starts.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So if there is anything that an agency needs to provide available to the public, there's a vehicle to get that into 311, and in turn, we get that into the system.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I always like to tout that for the public, what's online and in the mobile app is written in a plain language standard, so it makes it fair and equitable for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And we have all in, we have over 7,000 discrete pieces of information in the system, all having gone through that process at one point or another.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks whether all 311 representatives are aware of the Office to End Gender-Based Violence and can direct calls. Morrisroe says reps rely on the content system and he believes the information is there but will confirm.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks if reps know Office to End Gender-Based Violence

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And so is it fair to say that all the 200 and some odd service representatives at this point are aware?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: The Office to End Gender-Based Violence is, if someone calls in asking for Office of Community Safety or whatever, that they'll understand, they know what that is, and they know how to direct it?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I can address that in terms of how our process works.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So, yes, as long as the information's in our system, the rep rep

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Representatives are trained on how to use the tool, how to use the system, and count on and rely on what we call the content, the content in that system.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So they would be able to search.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: As long as it's in our system, they would have information in a standard structured way, and they can give that to the public.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But it's in the system, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: To my knowledge, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I would have to be double checking.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You can just confirm.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That'll just be helpful for us to confirm.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks about the app's AI Smart Select tool, whether it was built in-house or by a vendor, and what personal data it captures. Morrisroe says it was built with an MWBE vendor, allows photo or text submissions, and falls under 311's privacy policy.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about AI Smart Select vendor and data privacy

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And then my next question, and I'm sure the chair will...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Kind of expand a little bit more, but I did I do have the app.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm living in Bushwick a frequent trash service requester On the I noticed that there's like the AI smart select.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Sorry this chair is malfunctioning.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Um, I

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you share a little bit about, and I think it's helpful, I think it's been helpful because I think for a long time, especially if you're putting in a complaint about trash, there was a lot of miscommunication about what is illegal dumping, what is just a dirty sidewalk versus a dirty street.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you share if that feature or if the AI smart select tool, was that designed in-house or did you all contract with a vendor and whether or not

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Yeah, whether you use the vendor.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And what information does this tool capture?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Because I think while you're putting it in, obviously it's prompting you to put your address, your information.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How much of that is the tool capturing and how much of your personal data is it holding on to?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And is it a different data privacy agreement than the standard 311 app?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate the user feedback in that situation.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I take your kind of the different points in kind of an order, if I can, if I can remember it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So first off, I'm glad you're using Smart Select.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I don't think it gives me a choice.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I want to be honest.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: If you go to the app, I think it's at the top.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's at the top, yes.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So a little bit of context behind that.
