utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I feel like we have a tremendous CX team at 311, a customer experience team.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And this is one of the things where over time, they're constantly looking at what more do we need to do?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: What else can we be doing?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we know a lot of people come to the mobile app.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We've seen it grow over the years, obviously the growth of smartphones.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But people like to submit things in different ways.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we were giving them one.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: What the Smart Select does is give them another way and actually gives them three other ways, right?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So if you go to it, pull it up, you can take a picture.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: You can use a picture.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: You can upload a picture.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: You can take a picture.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And now you can actually type in some text about a condition you're seeing, you're near, you can observe.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The smart select will then determine what it is.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: You confirm and then you submit it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So now you don't have to go through the step of having to fill out a form because it's doing it for you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The work to do that was done by a combination of the OTI organization and its contracted MWBE vendor.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the vendor?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I know we call it an MWB vendor, so I don't know the name offhand.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Oh, that's the most generic.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, we'll follow up.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm sure I shall get that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And that went into effect last year.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The text was just an enhancement this year.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But the picture version was last year.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then very much falls under the same purview of privacy.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We are very serious about privacy at 311.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I personally believe it's what drives the public trust in 311 and has over 20 plus years.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That is very important to us.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So any tool that we use falls under that same purview with OTI and 311's privacy policy.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Chair De La Rosa returns to agency closures, citing noise complaints routed to NYPD that appear closed without resolution. She asks whether 311 was originally a call center model and whether there is any mechanism to hold agencies accountable.
chapters.title: De La Rosa questions agency accountability for closing 311 tickets

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So I want to ask sort of a question that follows the frame of thought of Councilmember Dinowitz and Riley around the closing of requests by agencies.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Obviously, none of us were here in 2003.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I was in high school.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I don't know what other people were.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So why is it that 311 was, like, when it was originally, I guess, put together, right?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Obviously, I know that there's limit in capacity.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But it doesn't feel like there is a system that speaks back to agencies for accountability if an agency is closing.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: A ticket, right?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I get it often in my community, like for noise complaints, right?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It gets rerouted to NYPD and NYPD goes out and they do whatever they do and then it appears closed and then constituents are telling us, hey, the issue was not resolved.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So is it more of like when 311 was imagined, it was a call center model?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Has there ever been a conversation about how to hold agencies better accountable to closing tickets?

chapters.summary: Morrisroe says intake sets expectations with 'what happens next' and due dates, and SLAs are published on Open Data. He says 311 has worked with NYPD to rewrite resolution descriptions in plain language so customers understand agency responses.
chapters.title: Morrisroe explains service level agreements and resolution descriptions

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I was also not there in 2003, but came shortly after.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So I can't speak to the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But I think there's three or four things that I can share that gets to what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But on an intake side, if I can do that first, there's a couple of things that happen, whether you're self-serving through the mobile app or online or whether you're talking to a call center representative.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: There's two key things that you'll get what we call the expectation.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And matter of fact, on the online, it says what happens next.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And that's a description of what happens next, which agency is going to respond and what the typical.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: turnaround time is or the due date to use that term.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Technically, we call those service level agreements.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So those are two things that happen on any service request interaction.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Then in addition to that, all the service level agreements that an agency that agencies have really with the city, right, with the public are available on open data.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: There's a list called 311 SLA.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So for every complaint, every complaint type, it will say what's the expected time to resolve.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That can be hours for some dire situations.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It can be days.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And in some cases, it can be longer than that because there are seasonal cycles.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's available.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then the other piece that talks to, I believe, what you're...

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Talking to is the aforementioned RSAT dashboard, where a customer can say, I opened this service request.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The agency told me, here's the status.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I get a request.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I can now say whether it is or not.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then that customer's point of view may be different than the agency's point of view.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: One of the things we try to do is define that, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So in the service request that the customer gets an update on, if they...

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Take the confirmation number if they get it emailed to them or if they call and look it up.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We have what we call a resolution description.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's a kind of a field and it's got a literal in it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Some of those do date back to 20 years.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So there's a work effort that started a couple of years ago that we tried to do.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We've done it successfully with NYPD, is to refine.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: those resolution descriptions, frankly, put them into plain language terms so the public can actually understand what the city is saying.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's something that has, we believe, has helped.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's hard to get data on that, but we believe it's helped to help just clarify that situation.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Like, what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: What does this agency response mean?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So those are a number of things we do where we can control that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And just all under the guise of trying to make it more informative and more understanding to the customer.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa notes a request can be closed on 311 while still open at DOT or Parks. Morrisroe says 311 does not close requests; agencies own status. Residents can check status with a confirmation number or through Open Data.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks how residents can see agency status after 311 closes

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I also think that it's important, like you mentioned, like setting expectations, because I think people think once you put in a 311 complaint, like I heard another agency say one time we're in a meeting.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Well, only because it's closed on 311 doesn't mean it's closed on the agency side.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But it would be great to like explain that to the person who's experiencing it.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Because they see the closed status and they think it's done.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: No one's following up.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It might be closed on 311, but at the DOT or at the Parks Department, it's still open.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Is there a mechanism right now where people can drop down and see that it's with the Parks Department and they're still working on it or no?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for describing that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I would say that just as a point of how we operate,

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: 311 doesn't close any requests.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So 311 opens and submits to the agency, but the agency owns all the status from that point on, whether it's in progress, updated, closed, or resolved, whatever term they may use.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But I agree with you with respect to informing more and more that we can, right?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Setting that expectation up front.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But yeah, the opportunity to see what's happening, there's at least two ways for the public.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: One is if you have the confirmation number.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Again, if you did it online, if you have an email, that's the best way to look it up.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: You can actually do it on the homepage of the app.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Just cut and paste your confirmation number, put it in, and it's going to give you the status.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: If you don't have that, you can contact 311.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's one way.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But also the open data portal, and I give a compliment out to my colleagues on the data analytics team at OTI who do a tremendous job with the open data portal for so many things in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But there's several rich 311 data sets on there.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The 311 service request data set is probably one of the most popular ones.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And that has a lot of information that can give you an update on your status of your complaint.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But also if there's a collection or, as Councilmember Riley had said, if there's a focus in a certain area in your neighborhood, that open data tool is really, really powerful.

chapters.summary: Chair asks whether 311 meets with agencies annually to review patterns. Morrisroe says reviews happen daily, quarterly, and annually through CX, quality assurance, agency analysts, and agency relations, with survey readouts shared with agencies.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about agency reviews and pattern analysis

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Is there like an end of year meeting where 311 sits with the agencies and it's like, these are the patterns we're observing?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Or once that data is sort of uploaded to the open data portal, is the expectation that the agencies kind of do that type of analysis for themselves?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I really appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: If you allow me to kind of brag on the teams at 311 and answering it, I'd appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That happens every day and it happens quarterly and it happens over the course of a year as well.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I alluded to earlier, we have a group that's called CX team.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: They look at the customer experience.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We have a quality assurance team making sure things are handled correctly.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We have the agency analyst.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We have.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Content writers, we have business relations.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So there's a lot of folks all focused on, are we doing it right today?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And how do we do it better tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that happens more on a workplace basis, but we do have structured reviews.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Some of our surveys get to that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We bring the whole team together.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We do the readout of the survey.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then our agency relations team carries that to their respective agency counterparts.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Chair notes the app is only in English and asks whether the entire app can be translated. Morrisroe says native app service request forms are English-only, but users can link to the mobile website and use Google Translate.
chapters.title: De La Rosa questions language access in the 311 app

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I do want to ask some questions about language access.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I do have some concerns about the app right now is just in English.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Can you speak to sort of is there a function to translate the entire app?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Like if you're a Spanish speaker, for example, and you want to access the app, like can you translate the app?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'll speak to that specifically.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So now the app has kind of two components to it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: What you see is there.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It is mobile optimized.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So if we link you to the 311 online, the website, then you have all the benefit of what's on the website, including the Google Translate tool.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: On the app itself, if you're using a service request and you're submitting a service request that's embedded in the app, we call that native to the app, that's in English only.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So it's something that only exists in English.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: If a customer does want to use the app, they can go to the mobile site.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'm sorry, go from the mobile site, quick link right to the website, and then use the website to be able to, one, translate.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: To the language they wish to and then access anything in that language.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So what's the challenge in making the app sort of just switch languages?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And it ties back to the work we do with the mobile app in total.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So whether it be trying to do better with the GPS, that Councilman Bedinowitz had reference to trying to find a better way of presenting the information and then just trying to do enhancements.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: There's a lot of work that constantly goes on in the mobile app, and it's just getting to that work.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair asks about an RFP on Passport for outsourced contact center services. Morrisroe says the current overflow vendor contract ends February 28, 2027, and the city is soliciting bids for a new contract starting March 1, 2027.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about RFP for outsourced contact center services

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, I do want to ask a few questions about passport procurement and other things.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: On the passport procurement website, there is an RFP for outsourced contract center services for NYC 311.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have the RFP number.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Please tell us more about the need for outsourcing the contact center.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for the question and for the context with respect to passport.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I thought you were going to ask me a passport question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So I'm glad it's a 311 question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So, yes, I can speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We talked previously about the contracted vendor, also known as the overflow vendor.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that contract ends February 27, February 28 of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The city approaches that we're going to solicit bids for a new contract that would start March 1st, 2027.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that, I'll call it the RFP that you referenced, that is to solicit vendors for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And so as of right now, you're just soliciting?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You're in the process of soliciting.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair references the August 18, 2026 911 outage after a Motorola update and asks about 311's update process. Morrisroe distinguishes IBM/application development from the Cisco telephony platform and says OTI now uses MWBE contracts for application work.
chapters.title: De La Rosa questions 311 software updates after 911 outage

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: On August 18, 2026, New York City experienced a significant 911 service disruption after Motorola, the city service provider, performed a routine software update.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Approximately 1,700 calls were impacted during that outage.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, IBM is the principal vendor supporting the 311 system.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And during...

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Prior testimony, you stated that a joint team of OTI, IBM is responsible for 311 system updates.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Can you walk us through the standard process for implementing software updates to 311?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for the context.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And yes, I can give you some of that perspective.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I probably can't go deep as some of my colleagues at OTI would, but I can give you a flavor of that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And I think the starting point would be to make a distinction.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So the work that we do with IBM and what was previously referenced, we do that for mostly for what we call applications development.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So for the system that you see online or the system that gets used in the call center, the application side of that, not the telephony system.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So those are two separate.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then most recently.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The telephone system.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So the telephone system is actually the source system.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The platform is a Cisco platform.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Cisco.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Which is pretty common across the city.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then back on the application side, as we in the past would have referenced IBM, the OTI is now using MWBE.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: e-contracts more so than the IBM contract.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that work, though, is similar.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We're contracting for specific skill sets and specific work that can help us develop and build out in our application.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: In some cases, you know, you bring it on, you help build it, and then you don't need it anymore.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But all of that gets overseen and managed by the OTI organization.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Morrisroe says software updates go through multiple approvals and change management, with backups and backups-to-backups. He says the 911 outage prompted review of procedures, and 311 evaluates emergencies through its own and NYCEM processes.
chapters.title: Morrisroe describes software update approvals and failover planning

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Obviously, you know, given what happened at 911, we have a few more questions about updates performed on the regular.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Are, you know, software updates of that nature happening on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Are they predetermined?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And then who determines when an update should occur and who within OTR or 301 must approve before it is deployed?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I get to expand a little bit on the work that we do.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So there are a number of levels of approval.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Software updates are very much our focus, as you can imagine, even without the reference to the earlier August event.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But this one, I would say, goes back 23 years as well.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's grounded in 301's approach that we must always be available.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And there's always times where you're going to have scheduled updates and scheduled outages.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Then you've got to have a backup, and you've got to have a backup to the backup.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's something that we take, whether it's the telecom side, whether it's the application side, take very serious.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And therefore, we have a number of processes in place.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'll just speak at a high level, and I have the privilege of also supporting the cities.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: internal customer service desk, the citywide service desk.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Within that team, there's a number of folks who focus solely on change management, as we call it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So I can kind of speak to that in both ways.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But there's always a need for software updates, software changes, software upgrades.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's a very controlled process.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The teams that need to do it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Put forth what they need to do.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: There's a body that understands what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So your change, you have to think about your change, but also will, in fact, somebody else's change.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: They all go through an approval process.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's pretty standard.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It can be on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It can be on a cycle basis.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But there's a pretty standard protocol of being able to go back and look at

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Here's the changes we need to make.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Here's why we need to make them.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And has everybody signed off on making those changes?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Since the 911 outage, has that prompted you all to review or change procedures governing software updates to 311?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I will say yes, because any event that occurs forces us to do just that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So this winter when we had extreme winter weather, this summer when we had heat waves,

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: you know, dating back, again, you mentioned the history of 311, but dating back to their earliest days when there was a transit strike in 2003.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That causes us to think about things, whether it's a natural disaster, whether it's a city, sorry, what's a technical change, but anything that occurs, we have a process through our emergency management resources on our team.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We also partner with

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: New York City Emergency Management, but within our own team, we'll evaluate.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: anything that is out of the norm and say, how would we handle this?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Are we covered?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Are we set?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Are we able to do that?

chapters.summary: Chair asks how 311 detects live failures, noting 911 dispatchers noticed problems manually. Morrisroe says 311 has system alerts and monitoring, including triggers if no calls are received for a set period, which email 24/7 staff.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about 311 failover alerts and detection

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So one of the questions that we asked of OTI when we were doing the 911 hearing was if there were any

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: redundancies or failover procedures, if something is failing, like live, like something is failing and someone like for the 911 outage, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Clear that something was failing until some of the 911 dispatchers began to notice things that were happening that were out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So can you walk us through what that looks like for the 311?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for the framing of that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we do have a number of alerts and flags that are designed from a system perspective, right?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So it's built into our operating systems are alerts, and then there's systems that do monitor just for alerts.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's a necessary requirement, somewhat of a standard requirement.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But we also have built in over the years tools that will alert us if something were to happen.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Our telecom platform is very robust.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It operates very well, but things can happen.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We have built in, I'll give just a simple example.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: If a call has not been received for X minutes, there's going to be a trigger and an alert and an email generated to one of our 24-7 operating people.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So during the course of a day,

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: know if that were to happen, it would be very quickly detected simply

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Because there's a lot of calls during the day.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But we also tweak it so even on the overnight when there may be gaps in calls because not a lot of people are calling, if we go for a certain period of time, minutes, there is a trigger and an email report and it goes to a live person to be able to say, now what do we do?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The city has a very structured process that OTI oversees.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I mentioned before the citywide service desk.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's the first step.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Open up a ticket.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Let's get everyone involved.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Let's start to understand what it is.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But the identification of that is something we have built in over the years.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair asks how many 311 operators are fluent in other languages. Morrisroe says only a small number speak Spanish in addition to English, and all other languages rely on third-party interpretation vendor LanguageLine.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about operator language fluency and LanguageLine

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Going back to language access, how many of your operators are fluent in other languages?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: In total, the only languages our operators speak other than English would be Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we have a small number of, I'll say, bilingual English-Spanish language speakers.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Everything else we rely on a third-party interpretation vendor, LanguageLine.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Language line.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair asks about staffing surges during emergencies. Morrisroe says 311 uses its contracted overflow vendor to quickly add trained staff, citing weather emergencies and the recent Nor'easter as examples.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about emergency surge staffing protocol

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: What is the current protocol if a need arises of having a staffing search of 311 call takers, such as during an emergency?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We do have a protocol for that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We've actually used it several times this year because of the weather emergencies that I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But this is where our contracted vendor resource comes into play more so than ever.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Because they do steady state work, they're already in the 311 program.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: They have the 311 systems.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: They have people who are trained on that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But we go to the vendor and say, we need more.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We need it quickly, and we need people who are qualified.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Because the vendor is a private organization and they have other business, they have the ability to have resources, right?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: They can have them available quickly.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we'll anticipate something's coming up.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: This past weekend, we had the Nor'easter.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: My executive director who runs the call center said, yep, weather's bad.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We're going to get more calls.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Let's see what we can do about adding some staff.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So if people are calling for downed trees, for example, we've got some additional staff to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we go to the vendor for that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: They can turn that resource up pretty quickly from their pool.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But then equally, they can then also take that resource down when it's needed.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that is our primary response to, that is our primary approach when it's responding to a surge.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We tend to call it a surge.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Chair asks about current AI plans. Morrisroe says AI is being explored to augment, not replace, call center representatives, including helping agents navigate or pre-populate information, building on older natural language screen-pop technology.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about AI plans for 311 app and website

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: My colleague, Councilmember Gutierrez, spoke a little bit of artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I just wanted to dig in more.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about your current plans for...

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: AI within 311 mobile app and website?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Like, what's the vision?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I do appreciate that one.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Like everyone, right, we're looking at how does that affect every aspect of the work that we do and what we deliver to the public.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we've had a few exercises and activities where we've worked and seen what AI can do.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We've had different demos that we've been able to take a look at.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we start with the principle, though, that AI working in our call center is designed to augment the work that the representative does, not replace the work that the representative does.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And we've seen a number of ways that can help.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: If AI can handle some, can help the agent identify how to navigate or be able to pre-pop something, or even

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: we have a very older version of it today that exists in our call center called natural language, where it can detect, if you interact with it, it can detect what you are asking about, and it'll do a screen pop for the rep to say, you know, it's a garbage recycle question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's 10 plus years old technology, but the concept behind that is what we look at with AI as well.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: How could AI help us better help the agent to better help the customer?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair asks why service requests are sometimes deemed outside an agency's jurisdiction. Morrisroe explains reassignments, often by design for cave-ins that DOT assesses before referring to another agency or utility, and says reassignments are about 1% of requests.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks why agencies mark requests out of jurisdiction

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, so I'm going to switch back to legislation-related questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I know that Councilmember Dinowitz asked about the geolocation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I think we have a good understanding of that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But I wanted to ask...

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Why might an agency determine that a service request is outside of

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: of their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It is my understanding that service requests are sent to agency based on the problem type.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So if the request is determined to be out of jurisdiction of the assigned agency, is that an issue of how the problem is set up at 311?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Like what is the genesis of the confusion?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Yes, that situation does exist, so I'm happy to be able to talk to that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We would, kind of a term we use is reassign service request in that situation.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So there's at least a couple of flavors to it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Some are by design, and it typically is something that happens where a customer is self-serving rather than if they call the call center.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The human aspect on the call center can help kind of put it in the right bucket.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But a very simple one is a cave-in on the street.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So to the public, it's a defect in the street, and I want to report it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And from a 301 perspective, we want to make that simple.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: For the agency to go fulfill on that, especially in infrastructure situations like that, it's not always clear who has authority on it because it's not, you know, a customer could describe it one way, but it could certainly be something different or the agency needs a different.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So by design, some of those complaint types go to DOT first.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: DOT does the assessment and then DOT may in turn assign it to another agency or utility that's contracted to go do that work.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's probably the most common one.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Some other ones may be, again, because a customer has described a situation and it'll get coded as such.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I can say it's relatively rare.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: While I appreciate the impact.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: those it does affect, just from a context perspective, it's about 1% of all service requests that go through a reassigned process.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair asks whether OTI tracks which problems are often marked out of jurisdiction, citing street cave-ins and traffic complaints. Morrisroe says the CX team analyzes reassignments and 311 is looking at improvements, but traffic bureau routing is an NYPD matter.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about out-of-jurisdiction patterns and traffic complaints

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Does OTI look into, like, which problems are often marked out of jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And if so, which requests are responded to?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Well, you already said that the street caving is the most popular one.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We heard from Deputy Speaker Williams, the one about traffic tends to be problematic as well with the Traffic Bureau versus the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Can you speak to some of that?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Yes, again, not maybe on the specific level or the traffic bureau one, because I think that would go to NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's just a matter within NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But we do look at that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: My CX team that I keep referring to have done analysis over the years, including recently, to look just at that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Do we have reassigned service requests?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Why do we have them?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: What could be done about it?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And as I said in the opening testimony, that's something we're looking into.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: How can we do that better?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And can three-on-one do more?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Can we enable an agency to do more?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And if it is a necessary step that has to happen, how can we make that better for the customer?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Is that data on the reassignment on open data?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It is embedded in open data.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I would say you can't, you know, it's not a field you can click on.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's going to give you the number that I just quoted, the 1%.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But in what I called the resolution description earlier, it'll have that in there that, you know, agency A has reassigned this to agency B.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair asks what happens when a request reaches the correct agency but wrong unit. Morrisroe says agencies often handle internal routing, but 311's agency relations team investigates recurring issues and may change forms or routing.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about requests sent to wrong unit within an agency

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Again, going back to the deputy speaker's question, but if a request is assigned to the correct agency, but the wrong unit within an agency, not, you know, I know NYPD is kind of a different situation, which we can talk about, but in any agency, what happens?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That can happen.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: There's probably two sides to that as well.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I can't speak to the agency side of that, but from familiarity, I can say a lot of the work that agencies do, their workflow is designed to handle it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But if it goes down a different pipe, let's say, it's within the same agency, they have the ability to communicate with each other in that respect to be able to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's a generic kind of observation, but it happens.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: What our role is, though, is if that is happening on a more of a one-off basis, the agency contacts their agency relations counterpart.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We dive into that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We'll look at it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And do we need to change the routing?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Is something changed on the agency side, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And if so, do we need to change the electronic form that goes to them to get it to the right workflow?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I imagine that happens often.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We get a lot of feedback, and then a lot of times we're digging into it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So I think a lot of the agencies are very mature in their processes, especially the infrastructure agencies who do this work on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So I think it's pretty standard, so much so that if it does happen and we get notified, it's more of a, oh, let's jump into this and figure it out because it's not the day-to-day.

chapters.summary: Chair mentions bills to add categories like dog runs and stolen SNAP benefits. Morrisroe explains categories can be added through legislation, internal gap analysis, public suggestions under Local Law 97, or agency requests, all assessed by 311 and agency partners.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks how new 311 complaint categories are added

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I alluded to earlier that we have a lot of bills that my colleagues want to hear on 311.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Some of them are to like.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: add categories, right?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Like I have one that is my pet peeve one, which is about dog runs.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Like we can't report stuff that's happening in dog runs right now.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: There's not a category for that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Can you walk us through the process of like, what would it take to add categories?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: That's a simple one, but some colleagues have bills, for example, around SNAP benefits being stolen, right?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Like things that are really critical for someone who's not getting a benefit from the city that they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So what's the process of adding a category?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I can definitely speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: There's a few different drivers that could trigger it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So yours is a great example, right?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And I assume we'll hear more in a future hearing on some of those suggestions.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But legislative driven is some.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Last year, there was a great partnership between the council and 311 and OTI to create the new cannabis retailer complaint.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we worked with council member Brewer and then the entire process.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's one way, right?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It gets brought up in that respect.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Our own team will figure it out.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Hey, there's something gapped here.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: There's something missing here.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We have a vehicle for the public to submit that situation.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Council passed local law 97 a couple of years ago.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's a process that the public can identify something.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then we'll put the 311 resources and the agency resources to assess it to see if it's needed.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then the agencies themselves, which is often a way to not only bring something new, but also to tweak something that may be in place.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So all of those are different ways, but they all at one point or another come into 311 as similar.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: to what we do with the public as intake.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We're going to assess that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We're going to confirm it's not in place.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then what does it look like it could be?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then work with the agency or work with the mayor's office and or work with council to be able to figure out how can we now get that into the system.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Chair asks whether the privacy policy has been updated and what user information is shared. Morrisroe says the policy was strengthened last year, 311 does not share user information, and contact details are only used to fulfill requests like heat complaints.
chapters.title: De La Rosa questions 311 privacy policy and data sharing

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Privacy and data.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So 311 privacy policy has.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And has been updated from last year?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Hasn't been updated, I guess is the question.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Could you share with us if there has been changes to prior policy?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for that one.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Yes, it has been.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I have to check myself on whether it's a year or a couple of months, you know, give or take.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But the privacy policy has been longstanding, as I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Last year, we took the opportunity to strengthen it on behalf of customers.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we put some language in specific to the section that speaks to how we use your data, how we won't use your data.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And I can't recall the exact language, but the goal of that was, as I said, to strengthen it on behalf of the customers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So the following questions were, it's kind of a follow-up, but the following questions were asked of our last committee hearing during which you respectfully offered to get back to the committee with answers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: One of the questions is, according to the privacy policy, 3-in-1 does not sell, rent, or otherwise use information for marketing purposes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So for what purposes do you share users'information?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: What third parties are receiving the user data?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And what kind of data is being sent and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'll do.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The first one, we don't share user information.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And it's something that's interesting with 311.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The user information, name, contact information, right, is very rare that it's needed.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Most of what you can do, you don't need to provide user information.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And that's by design.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Again, going back to the history of 311, because it then contributes to helping people feel comfortable and confident to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But we do have limits around what can be shared.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's really in the interest of fulfilling that service request.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So if you want to make a heat complaint, you can do that without giving your name.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: If you want to make a heat complaint in your apartment, then the HPD needs your contact information.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So you'll include that, but that information is not shared then with third parties.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And so even your contractors, your third-party contractors, any information that is picked up in any of those scenarios is not shared.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So there are strict protocols to prevent that from happening.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair asks whether mobile app data is encrypted in transit, whether users can delete data, and whether a retention policy exists. Morrisroe says he will follow up on encryption and deletion, and agrees conceptually to work on a retention policy.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about app encryption, deletion, and retention

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Can OTI ensure that the mobile app data is encrypted in transit, or is that up to another party?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'm pausing because I don't know if I can give you a definite answer, but OTI could give you a definite answer.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: If I can get back to you on that, I'd feel more comfortable.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So we'll follow up with that one.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And then can OTI allow for user data from 311 app to be deleted if requested?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'd like to take that same approach, if you don't mind, if I can just get back to you so I can make sure we get to you the correct.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So when looking at the privacy policy, there is no set retention policy listed for personal information except for voice recordings, meaning that personal information is possibly stored indefinitely.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We retain user information for as long as it's necessary to fulfill user submitted requests or to provide ongoing assistance to a user.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If a user has set up an account with 311 contact center, the user's information will be retained until the user deletes the account.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: For compliance reasons, some users'information may be retained after deletion of the account.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: That's a quote from the privacy policy.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Would you agree that we should set a data retention policy for personal information?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I appreciate that question, and I appreciate you mentioning on the voice side there is a purging period.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Say that again.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: On the voice side.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Sorry, the call center side.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Recordings, the voice recordings.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And conceptually, yes, I think we should look at that, and we'd be happy to work with you on that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you think...

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, I think you answered our questions.

chapters.summary: Chair asks why domain names are collected and whether the cookie banner lets users opt out of non-essential cookies. Morrisroe says he prefers to have OTI experts provide accurate answers and will follow up.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about domain names and cookie opt-out

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: According to the privacy policy, the domain names associated with a user's device are collected.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: What is the purpose of the collection?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for that one.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I think I would prefer to be able to get back to you if you don't mind, because the answer I'm going to give you is based on my knowledge, but I'd rather get our experts to give me the answer to give to you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I imagine it's the same reply, but for the cookies.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Does the cookie banner to provide options for users to opt out from using the non-essential cookies?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you plan to provide that option for New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: With respect, I would appreciate being able to do that and get back to you on that one.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So those are more like OTI questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I've talked to my colleagues who are very proficient in that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair recalls past testimony about extending 311 to WhatsApp. Morrisroe says it has not launched yet, remains on the roadmap, and challenges include estimating demand, staffing, and reconciling WhatsApp privacy terms with 311 policy.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about WhatsApp channel roadmap

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So let's talk a little bit about future plans.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: According to your testimony, on June 30th, 2022 and 2023, 311 will extend services to the WhatsApp messaging platform.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Further, on April 25, 2024, you confirmed those plans as it's still part of the roadmap for 311.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Did it happen?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It has not happened yet.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We have a WhatsApp account, but we have not moved it forward to make it a channel, make it publicly available.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So it's still on our roadmap and still work in progress.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: What are some of the challenges there?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: A couple of different challenges.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It's a new channel for us, and we don't have a good baseline on what kind of volume we would have.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Obviously, we size it based on what we can.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So we really have to figure out if we open that channel or when we open that channel up, what is going to be the demand, and then how do we staff up to meet that demand.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We don't want to be understaffing it, and especially if we're going to, even if we launch it on a pilot basis, we want to be able to make sure we can handle what comes in.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's one of the pieces.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then working through the process with the WhatsApp tool itself is something that we're very

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Cognizant of.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So how would the WhatsApp privacy policy and terms of agreements align with 311 privacy policies?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you know?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I can't answer the question, but I can tell you that that's one of the things that we're looking at as far as the roadmap.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: How do we reconcile those two things?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Chair asks for the end-to-end process under Local Law 97. Morrisroe says public suggestions come to 311, are reviewed by Customer Relations, then agency relations, and agencies decide whether to add a service request; 311 reports annually on progress.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about Local Law 97 process for new complaint types

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Going into complaint types, local law 97 of 2022, can you walk us through from the beginning to the end the process for creating a new complaint or service request type for 311, which we kind of talked about a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarifying specific to the local law 97 process or.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So since local law 97 has been in effect, the public can recommend or suggest or request a service request.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I'm kind of generalizing that, but there's a vehicle where they can do that.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: It comes into 311.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We have a team that receives that and does the initial intake on it.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And basically everything that comes in is considered the starting point, right?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But then that gets logged in a tool within 311.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: After that assessment, it goes to our agency relations team who then talks to their agency counterparts.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa

chapters.summary: Chair asks about the dynamic between 311 and NYPD when complaints are not fulfilled. Morrisroe says 311 focuses on accurate intake and routing, calibrates regularly with NYPD, and has a dedicated NYPD liaison, but defers to NYPD on outcomes.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about NYPD, 311, and 911 relationship

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I want to ask a few questions about NYPD and sort of the relationship between NYPD 311911.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So you testified earlier that, I mean, I'm saying it seems like there's some challenges in terms of oversight at NYPD because that's a different operation, right?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Can you explain sort of the dynamic between your 311 operation and NYPD when there are complaints that are directed towards NYP that are not fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: What I can speak to is the three-on-one side in terms of the intake that we do.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Our goal then is to make sure we're getting the information accurate.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The forms are working.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We calibrate with NYPD on a regular basis to make sure they're getting routed correctly.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So that's where we put our energy and our focus.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We have feedback mechanisms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa

chapters.summary: Chair asks whether emergency calls to 311 are automatically routed to 911. Morrisroe says training reinforces hot transfers to 911 when there is any suggestion of emergency, with the mantra 'when in doubt, route,' and contracted vendors follow the same protocol.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about emergency transfers from 311 to 911

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: I do appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: That's one of the things that we

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So it does happen.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Someone could call 311 not knowingly or just choosing to call 311.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: In short order, we train and reinforce and reinforce to, if any suggestion of an emergency, any suggestion of anything dangerous, threat, incident.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Transfer to 911.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: We actually call it a hot transfer because all they do is hit a button and then the 911 operator comes on.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: So our approach is get that to the expert, get that to 911, let them make the determination if it's an emergency or not.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: When in doubt, route.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The professional at 911 is making that determination.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And I'm assuming that your training for the call center staff is robust in that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In that area?

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: The training itself is very robust.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: And then even our contracted vendors follow the same protocol.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: But it is something that is reinforced.

utterances.speaker: Joe Morrisroe
utterances.text: As I said, I think literally day one of training, if not day one, day two, because it's so important.

chapters.summary: Chair asks whether 311 has a public education or PSA budget like Notify NYC. Morrisroe says 311 works closely with Notify NYC but has no marketing or outreach budget, which the chair says is worth examining in future budget hearings.

summary: Committee on Technology held an oversight hearing on NYC 311 and three bills: Intro 173 on GPS coordinates, Intro 669 on traffic complaint routing, and Intro 800 on redirecting service requests.

OTI Deputy Commissioner Joe Morrisroe testified on 311 operations, staffing, outsourcing, language access, privacy, and software updates, answering questions from Chair De La Rosa and Councilmembers Dinowitz, Riley, Gutierrez, and Schulman.
Public witnesses Ms. Jennings and Chaudhry Hassan Mahmood raised concerns about unresolved 311 complaints and fire safety complaint routing before the hearing adjourned.
